section_summary: This section contains several duplicate or partial copies of Kilsoo K. Haan’s polemical article “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii,” together with the Sino-Korean Peoples League’s July 1939 cover letters transmitting it to Congress, Under Secretary Sumner Welles, and President Franklin D. Roosevelt. The article portrays Japanese cultural, religious, educational, consular, and economic activity in Hawaii as a coordinated threat to Americanization and Pacific security, and advocates an embargo on war materials and support for China and Korea. State Department routing memoranda record the Department’s handling and proposed acknowledgment of Haan’s correspondence.

subfiles.title: Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii — concluding pages of an earlier copy
subfiles.about: The concluding portion of Haan’s article argues that Japanese institutions and loyalties in Hawaii endanger American security and recommends measures against Japanese militarism.
subfiles.summary: Concluding pages of Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii: racial competition, the Fushimi scholarship fund, alleged Japanese influence over Hawaii's people of Japanese ancestry, and Haan's call for an embargo on war materials.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on filing letters from Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.from: E. G. C., Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: An internal note states that Haan’s letters normally are filed without acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: the Department's practice is to file Kilsoo Haan's letters without replying, so the attached letters are marked for filing.

subfiles.title: Instruction to acknowledge Haan’s correspondence
subfiles.about: The Under Secretary asks Hamilton to prepare an appropriate acknowledgment of Haan’s communication.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum referring Haan's correspondence to Hamilton; the Under Secretary, contrary to the filing practice, asks for an acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to Sumner Welles
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples League
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Haan sends Welles a copy of the article and urges a more positive American response to Japanese activity in the Pacific and Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: Haan sends Welles his article Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii, recently given to Senate committees, calling Japanese aggression a long-predicted threat and asking for a positive American policy.

subfiles.title: Submission of “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to Senate committees
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples League of Hawaii
subfiles.to: Members of the Senate Foreign Relations, Naval, and Military Committees, Seventy-Sixth Congress
subfiles.about: Haan submits the article to Senate committees and compares the strategic vulnerability of Guam and Hawaii with Korea’s subjugation by Japan.
subfiles.summary: Letter to Senate committees stressing Hawaii's strategic value, citing a study that Guamanians fear Japanese rule, and arguing the powers ignored Korean warnings.

subfiles.title: Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii
subfiles.about: Haan presents Japanese cultural and political activity in Hawaii as part of an expansionist national program threatening the United States’ first line of defense.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet traces Japanese expansion across Asia and the Pacific and alleges that Japan could use island bases, fishing fleets, and Hawaii’s Japanese population in a future conflict with the United States. It reviews Japanese diplomatic pressure on Hawaii, the Prince Fushimi scholarship fund, Christianity, dual nationality, expatriation, and Japanese-language schools as instruments of continuing Japanese influence. Its conclusion links the alleged Japanization of Hawaii with Japanese militarism and recommends an embargo on war supplies together with moral support for China and Korea.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples League
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States
subfiles.about: Haan sends President Roosevelt the article and appeals for an active American policy toward Japanese activities in the Pacific and Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: Haan sends Roosevelt his article, given to Senate committees, describing Japanese aggression as a realized threat and seeking a positive American response.

subfiles.title: Submission of “Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii” to Senate committees — duplicate copy
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan, Sino-Korean Peoples League of Hawaii
subfiles.to: Members of the Senate Foreign Relations, Naval, and Military Committees, Seventy-Sixth Congress
subfiles.about: A duplicate submission letter invokes Guam’s desire for fortification and warns that Guam and Hawaii could suffer Korea’s fate under Japanese domination.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate letter to Senate committees emphasizing Hawaii's strategic value, Guam's fear of Japanese domination, and Korea's ignored warnings.

subfiles.title: Japanization, A Peril to Hawaii — second copy, incomplete
subfiles.about: A second copy of Haan’s pamphlet begins with its preface and continues through the opening of the discussion of Japanese-language schools.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet portrays Japan’s territorial expansion and Pacific island holdings as preparations for possible action against Hawaii and the American Pacific Coast. It recounts Japanese diplomatic interventions in nineteenth-century Hawaii and describes “duck diplomacy,” racial tensions, the Prince Fushimi fund, Japanese Christianity, and dual nationality as elements of Japanization. The surviving copy ends during the argument that Japanese-language schools teach Japanism and impede Americanization.
